text:
# Eleven

The protest had come in at 5:45 on Friday, which was when protests came in, and Owen Castellano had read it standing up in his kitchen with his coat still on. Now it was Sunday night and he was reading it again at his desk at home, with the rest of the bid file fanned out around it, and the house was quiet in the way it got after ten.

He had been doing this for twenty-two years. Kestrel Ridge Unified was a good client, the kind that called before it did something instead of after, and Dale Ruffin, its facilities director, was a good man who wanted one thing from his lawyer, which was to be told that the project was fine. The project was the middle school, Buildings B and C: a new fire sprinkler system in both buildings, new rooftop HVAC, new electrical service and switchgear, fire alarm, roofing, doors, finishes. Thirteen and a half million dollars of Measure KR bond money. The Board was to award it Tuesday night. The Board met once a month.

Four bids. The low bidder was Corvane Builders, out of Modesto, at $13,412,000. Second was Tasker & Moye, at $13,699,000. Tasker & Moye was local; Bill Tasker had been in town forty-one years and was at that moment sixty percent of the way through building the District's new stadium, with a $612,000 change order for bad soil under the track sitting on Dale's desk, unresolved. The gap between the two bids was $287,000. Theo in Business Services had already said what $287,000 was. It was two portables.

The protest was from Gwen Talbot, at Talbot Mercer, for Tasker & Moye. Three grounds. He had them nearly by heart.

One: Corvane wasn't licensed for the work. The job included a fire sprinkler system and an HVAC replacement, and Corvane held a Class B general building license and nothing else. Its subcontractor list named an electrician, a plumber, a fire alarm outfit, a roofer, and a painter, and said everything else would be performed by the bidder. No sprinkler sub. No HVAC sub. Talbot said a B couldn't do either trade itself, and that a bid by a contractor not licensed for the work was nonresponsive and had to be rejected, and she quoted the statute that said so.

Two: Corvane hadn't acknowledged Addendum 2. Addendum 2 had changed the locksets on fourteen classroom doors to the classroom-security function. Eighteen thousand dollars, Talbot said. Corvane's bid form initialed Addendum 1 and left the second line blank.

Three: Copper Basin Unified, the district next door, had terminated Corvane for cause in March 2024 on a gym job, and its board had ratified the termination in open session, five to nothing. Not a responsible bidder.

The associate, Maya Ellery, had sent a first-look memo Friday night that was better than most first looks. She had pulled the sections Talbot cited and set them out in full, and she had ended with the question that was the whole case, though he wasn't sure she knew it. A nonresponsive bid can be rejected on its face, she wrote. A responsibility question gets notice and a hearing first. I haven't researched which this is.

He had.

The HVAC point was noise. Section 7057 said a general building contractor could do or superintend the whole or any part of a project that required two or more unrelated trades, and this one required five. A B could put rooftop units on a school. Talbot knew that, or should have. It was in the letter because licensing was the most common protest ground in the state and you threw it in.

The sprinklers were different, and he had been turning them over for two days. Subdivision (c) of the same section said a general building contractor shall not contract for any project that includes a fire protection system unless it holds the fire protection classification or subcontracts the work to someone who does. Corvane held a B. Corvane had listed no one. On the face of the bid, Corvane was going to install a fire sprinkler system in two school buildings with its own forces, and the statute said it could not contract to do that.

And yet. The District's own instructions to bidders had asked for a Class B license and nothing else. Section 7.1, in bold. Corvane had one. On the face of the bid, Corvane had met every requirement the District had set. The general rule, the one he had given to a hundred clients, was that if you had to go outside the four corners of the bid to find the problem, it was a responsibility problem, and responsibility got the bidder notice and a hearing before the Board could pass it over. Whether Corvane could lawfully do the sprinkler work was a question about Corvane, not about the bid.

Except the other statute, the one Talbot had quoted in full, said that a bid submitted by a contractor who is not licensed in accordance with this chapter shall be considered nonresponsive and shall be rejected, and that the agency shall verify, before award, that the contractor was properly licensed when it bid. Not licensed in accordance with this chapter. He had read the sentence perhaps forty times. Did it mean a contractor with no license at all, the handyman with a pickup, the thing the section was obviously written for? Or did it mean a contractor without the license this project needed? Properly licensed. Properly for what? He could argue it either way, and he could hear Talbot arguing it the other way, at the podium, Tuesday, with the Courier's education reporter in the second row.

And there was the thing underneath, the thing nobody would write down. Dale wanted the project. Dale wanted the 27th. The switchgear and the rooftop units were running thirty to thirty-six weeks from order and had to be released by the first of December or the electrical and the HVAC slid to summer 2028, a year lost, with the Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee meeting in January. Dale had also, without ever saying so, wanted Bill Tasker, who was building his stadium and whose change order he had not yet decided on. And Corvane had bid two portables less than Bill Tasker, and was the low bidder, and the law was for the low bidder.

Dale's recommendation to the Board was due in the packet supplement at one o'clock Monday. Corvane's response to the protest, if it sent one, wasn't due until Tuesday. He would be writing before he knew what Corvane had to say.

He had a legal pad. On it he had written *sprinklers* and underlined it, and under that, *face of the bid?*, and under that, *"not licensed in accordance with this chapter"*, and under that nothing. The desk lamp made a circle on the pad and the rest of the room was dark. He had meant to go to bed an hour ago. He had meant to have an answer.

He put his head down on his folded arms, just for a minute, the way he had in law school, with the lamp still on and the protest letter under his elbow, and the sprinklers and the fence of the statute and Bill Tasker's forty-one years went around once more, slower, and then let go of each other.

He was asleep before the thought finished.

* * *

The thought finished, but the room did not wait for it to land. The desk lamp stretched, its metal neck unspooling like a ribbon of gold thread that went under the floorboards and out into the yard, where it hooked onto the fence posts and pulled the whole yard toward the house. The fence was made of water now, a low wall of blue glass that hummed with the frequency of a transformer, and Owen could hear the water running through the pipes inside it, a sound like a thousand tiny bells ringing in a jar.

He tried to lift his head, but his arms were roots. They had gone down through the wood of the desk, through the drywall of the house, into the dark earth where the soil was soft and warm like a wool blanket. He looked down at the legal pad. The word *sprinklers* was no longer ink; it was a puddle of silver mercury that was slowly eating the paper, spreading its legs, turning the word *face* into a hole. Through the hole, he could see the middle school, but the school was underwater. The windows were bubbles.

Dale Ruffin was there, but he was not Dale. He was a giant made

of red brick and mortar, his face a smooth panel of unglazed tile that reflected nothing, not even the moon that hung so low it seemed to be resting on the tips of the school's football goalposts. The goalposts were made of copper wire, and they were buzzing, a high-pitched sound that vibrated in Owen's teeth.

"The bid is the soil," the brick man said, but his voice did not come from a mouth. It came from the ground itself, a rumble that shook the roots of Owen's arms loose from the earth. "You cannot build on a fault line if you do not know where the line is."

Owen looked at the bid file. The pages had turned into leaves, thin and green and veined with veins that looked like circuit boards. He tried to pick one up, but it dissolved into a swarm of moths that fluttered past his ear, their wings made of the tiny, printed words of the statute. *Section 7057.* The moths were saying it over and over, a chorus of rustling paper.

The dusty ledger revealed a secret accounting of stolen funds from decades ago. The sunlight danced off the shimmering surface of the fresh loom as she unwrapped her newest scarf of pure silk. The ancient swamp breathed slowly as foggy mist curled over its rotting roots and silent, murky water.

Owen watched the ledger open itself, its spine cracking like a dry bone, and the pages blew out not as paper but as a flock of dry leaves that landed in the swamp water, turning instantly into coins. Each coin was stamped with the face of a school bus, and they sank with a heavy, metallic chime that echoed up through the water and into the brick man's chest, where it rattled like change in a pocket.

"The silk is the soil," the man said, and the scarf unfurled from the woman's hands, stretching across the water, turning into a bridge of woven grass that connected the underwater school to the brick man. Owen tried to step onto the bridge, but his feet were made of the copper wire from the goalposts, sparking against the grass.

The swamp water rose, filling the room, the house, the world, and it was warm and smelled of ozone and old glue. The water did not wet the desk; it passed through it as if the wood were a ghost, but it made the legal pad heavy, dragging the silver puddle of the word *sprinklers* toward the edge of the page. As it slid, the letters untangled and reformed into the shape of a valve, a brass gate that clicked open with a sound like a gavel falling.

Through the valve, the water poured not down, but up, defying gravity to fill the space between the ceiling and the floor until they were the same thing. The ceiling was now the grassy roof of the middle school, dotted with the copper wire goalposts that hummed louder now, vibrating the coins in the swamp below.

Dale's brick face began to crack, not with violence, but like a drying riverbed, revealing not bone or flesh inside, but the copper piping of the new fire suppression system. The weary farmer drove his iron plow through the frozen mud, leaving deep furrows in the silent, snow-draped landscape. The plow was not iron; it was the spine of the ledger, heavy and rusted, and the furrows it cut were not in snow but in the silver mercury of the *sprinklers* on the page. As it carved, the snow-draped landscape rose up to become the white ceiling of the school, and the deep furrows became the trenches where the copper pipes would be laid, glowing faintly in the dark.

The travelers stepped from the scorching desert into an oasis where lush palm trees and crystal-clear pools offered a moment of serene relief. The desert was the drywall of the office, stripped of its paint, hot and brittle. The travelers were not people, but the four bids, four distinct colors of smoke that swirled together before solidifying into the oasis. The palm trees were the rooftop HVAC units, their fronds made of green circuitry that rustled with the sound of air moving through ducts. The tiny, sticky bandage wrapped tightly around her scraped knee seemed to hold back all the pain from the sharp fall. But the knee was not a knee; it was the corner of the bid file where the paper had been torn by the brass valve, and the bandage was a strip of red tape that glowed with a heat that did not burn. It held the tear shut, but the tear was breathing, expanding and contracting with the rhythm of the copper pipes in the brick man's chest.

The oasis shimmered, and the crystal-clear pools turned into the faces of the Board members, but their eyes were missing, replaced by the blank, white spaces of the uninitialed Addendum 2. They stared up at Owen, their mouths open, but instead of voices, they exhaled the dry, hot wind of the desert. The wind carried the scent of burning rubber and old dust, the smell of a school building left empty for a year.

"You are late," the wind said, and the voice was the sound of the moths flapping their wings. "The soil has shifted."

The massive turbine at the wind farm hummed so loudly against the twilight that it seemed to hold the entire mountain in its ceaseless spin. The mountain was the hill of the Kestrel Ridge campus, but it was made of the thick, gray binders of the bid files, stacked so high they scraped the twilight, which was not the sky but the ceiling of the District's parking garage. The turbine was the fan of the rooftop HVAC unit, spinning so fast it became a blur of silver, and its hum was the sound of the statute being read backwards, a thousand voices reciting *Section 7057* over and over until the words lost their meaning and became just a vibration that shook the coins in the swamp.

The old man wiped the thick, salty sweat from his brow as he navigated the foggy morning market. The old man was Bill Tasker, but he was also the brick man, and his brow was the face of the stadium, the concrete bleachers sweating salt that fell into the swamp and turned the water into brine. The market was the Board meeting room, but the stalls were lined with the copper wire goalposts, and the merchants were selling not fruit or bread, but change orders

The change orders were not paper. They were heavy, wet stones that the merchants handed over with silent, open palms. Each stone bore the number of the job in raised, rusted iron: *$612,000*. When Owen touched one, it burned cold, and he felt the track under the stadium shift, the soil sliding away like wet sand in an hourglass, revealing the hollow, empty space where the foundation should have been.

The old wooden spindle spun rapidly in the girl's hands, weaving her grandfather's stories into a tapestry of gold and green. The girl was Maya, but her face was blank, a smooth oval of white porcelain, and her hands were made of the same copper wire that held the goalposts together. The spindle was the brass valve from the page, turning so fast it became a silver blur, and the stories it wove were not words but the blueprints of the school, the lines of the fire sprinklers crossing and crossing again until they formed a net.
